summary: Presents a base YANG data model for managing Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) protocols that use connectionless communication. It is technology independent and written in YANG as specified in RFC 7950. Technology-specific models can extend it. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: This is a common checklist for testing networks where messages are sent without first setting up a dedicated path, like dropping letters in a mailbox. Different test tools can all fill in the same form.

questions: yang oam model for ping and traceroute
what is a test point in oam
subtitle: A shared YANG data model for configuring and reading ping-style network diagnostics that need no set-up connection.

tldr.problem: Different networking technologies have grown similar but separate OAM toolsets (ping, traceroute and the like), so managing them means learning a different data model for each.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8532 defines a technology-independent YANG base model with test points, the tools they support, neighboring test points, and generic path discovery and Continuity Check data. Technology-specific models extend it by augmenting it or by mounting their own modules.
tldr.outcome: Operators get one uniform way to describe connectionless OAM, and technology models such as BFD or LSP ping can plug into it. It is a Proposed Standard and is not obsoleted.

facts.label: Location types
facts.value: IPv4, IPv6, MAC, AS number, router-id

today: RFC 8532 is a Proposed Standard from April 2019 and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its connection-oriented counterpart is RFC 8531, and its data retrieval companion is RFC 8533.

sections.title: Why a Generic OAM Model
sections.content:
OAM (Operations, Administration, and Maintenance) covers the functions that let operators monitor communications with reachability verification and Continuity Check, troubleshoot failures through fault verification and localization, and monitor service-level agreements and performance. Ping and Traceroute, as in RFC 792 and RFC 4443, are the well-known examples for IP networks, and over the years different technologies have developed similar toolsets.

The RFC separates two families. In connection-oriented technologies a connection is set up before data flows. In connectionless technologies data is typically sent without prior arrangement, but control information is needed to identify the destination. A model for the connection-oriented case is in RFC 8531; this document covers the connectionless case.

The model is written in YANG (RFC 7950) and includes only configuration and state data. It can be used together with the data retrieval method model in RFC 8533, which covers procedures such as RPCs, or independently of it.
sections.eli5: Many kinds of networks have their own tools to check whether messages can get through. This document writes down one shared way to describe those checks so they all look alike.

sections.title: How the Model Is Organized
sections.content:
The model is split into two YANG modules. The ietf-lime-time-types module holds common time-related and timestamp-related definitions. The ietf-connectionless-oam module holds the technology-independent abstraction of key OAM constructs.

The second module augments the /networks/network/node path from the ietf-network module (RFC 8345) with a test-point-locations grouping. A test point (TP) is a functional entity at a node that can initiate and react to OAM diagnostic tests; the document focuses on data-plane functionality.

Each entry in a test-point-locations list carries a test-point-location-info grouping, which is built from three pieces: tp-technology for OAM technology details, tp-tools for the supported tools, and connectionless-oam-tps for how this test point relates to others. The tp-address and tp-address-ni groupings are kept outside it so that it stays addressing agnostic. At the top of the model a cc-oper-data container holds session statistics, which apply only to proactive OAM sessions.
sections.eli5: The model is like a filing cabinet with two drawers. One drawer holds the kinds of clocks and time units. The other holds the description of the places in the network where tests can happen.

sections.title: Test Point Addresses and Locations
sections.content:
With connectionless OAM, a test point can be identified in one of four ways: a MAC address at the data-link layer, an IPv4 or IPv6 address at the IP layer, a TP-attribute that identifies a test point tied to an application-layer function, or a router-id that stands for the whole device.

To define how a test packet is forwarded, the address needs extra parameters such as DSCP for IP or Traffic Class for MPLS. The generic model deliberately does not configure these; the model user adds them as needed.

The tp-location-type leaf picks the kind of location, for example ipv4-location-type or ipv6-location-type. Under each type a container holds a list keyed by the test point address, the location information, and, where required, a network instance name such as a VRF instance name. The full hierarchy has IPv4, IPv6, MAC, AS number and router-id location types.
sections.eli5: To test a spot in the network you need to say where it is. The model lets you name the spot by its street number (an IP address), its hardware name tag (a MAC address), or the name of the whole building (a router-id).

sections.title: Tools, Neighbors and Retrieved Data
sections.content:
OAM tools are activated in one of two ways. Proactive OAM runs continuously to report faults and needs persistent configuration. On-demand OAM is started by manual intervention for a limited time and needs only transient configuration. The session-type grouping says which kind a session uses, and its default is on-demand.

The tp-tools grouping holds two booleans, continuity-check and path-discovery. They describe the toolset for fault detection and isolation and can act as a constraint when the base model is extended. For example, configuring ICMP PING means setting continuity-check to true and then augmenting the model with ICMP PING details.

Because communication stacks have several layers, one interface can present several test points. Each test point can list its oam-neighboring-tps in other layers up and down the stack. The position leaf is -1 for a neighbor placed before the current test point, 1 for one placed after, and 0 when there is none.

Two generic groupings describe data that can be retrieved by any method, including RPC operations. Path discovery data has source and destination test point containers, a sequence number, a hop count, session statistics, path verification and path trace information, with per-hop items such as timestamps and ingress and egress interface names. Continuity Check data is similar without the per-hop trace. None of the fields are mandatory, so different retrieval methods can use them.
sections.eli5: Some checks run all the time, like a smoke alarm, and some you do only when you smell smoke. The model also lets a test spot point to its neighbors above and below, so you can follow a problem up and down the layers.

sections.title: Extending the Base Model
sections.content:
The base model is meant to be extended with technology-specific details. Section 6 of the RFC shows this for BFD and LSP ping. It states that its snippets are for illustration and that complete extensions should be worked out in the working groups of the respective protocols.

There are two methods. With the augment method, a module adds a technology type (the RFC example adds a bfd or lsp-ping leaf under technology), adds nodes to a test-point-locations list, or adds a new location-type case such as one for BFD over MPLS TE. Existing groupings from the dedicated BFD or LSP ping models can be reused to avoid duplicated effort.

With the schema mount method (RFC 8528), the test-point-locations list has a root attribute defined as an anydata node and a mount point. Other OAM YANG modules, such as the BFD single-hop and multihop modules or the LSP ping module, can then be populated in the schema-mounts container without any special change to the base module. The RFC notes one limitation: it is not possible to specify that certain modules are required to be mounted under a mount point.
sections.eli5: The base model is a plain LEGO board. A team that cares about one kind of test can snap its own bricks on, either by changing the board a little or by clicking in a ready-made piece.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module defines a schema for data accessed through management protocols such as NETCONF (RFC 6241) or RESTCONF (RFC 8040). The mandatory-to-implement secure transport is SSH for NETCONF and TLS for RESTCONF, and the NETCONF Access Control Model (RFC 8341) can restrict users to a subset of operations and content.

The writable data nodes are the five test-point-locations lists, one per location type. Unauthorized write access to them can adversely affect how an OAM management system handles end-to-end OAM and coordinates OAM within underlying network layers, which may lead to inconsistent configuration, reporting and presentation.

Some readable nodes may also be sensitive. The RFC lists the IPv4 and IPv6 session statistics counters (session-count, session-up-count, session-down-count and session-admin-down-count) and says read access to them should be controlled.
sections.eli5: The settings in this model decide how a network is tested, so only trusted people should be allowed to change them. Some of the test results are also private enough that not everybody should be allowed to peek at them.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC registers two URIs in the IETF XML Registry: urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-lime-time-types and urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-connectionless-oam.

It also registers the two modules in the YANG Module Names registry. ietf-lime-time-types uses the prefix lime, and ietf-connectionless-oam uses the prefix cl-oam.
sections.eli5: The new module names were written in an official name book so no one else uses the same names by accident.
